messages.subject: Re: jitter in layer() syntax
messages.body_plain:
On Apr 15, 6:02 pm, Jacob Wegelin <jacobwege...@fastmail.fm> wrote:
> What do the "width" and "height" attributes of jitter really do? The example below seems to demonstrate that setting these attributes to zero does *not* remove the jitter.

> print(
>         ggplot() + layer2
>         + scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=0, labels="")
>         )
> #       "expand" seems to control the amount of vertical space around the points.
> #       Incidentally, how would I get rid of the tick on the y axis?

Setting breaks=NA should get rid of all of the y-axis display,
including labels, tick marks, and lines:

ggplot() + layer2 + scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1),

breaks=NA)

>
> #       If we set both jitter parameters to zero, there should be no jitter at all.
> layer2<-layer(
>         data=DAAT
>         , mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
>         , geom="point"
>         , geom_params=list(shape=1)
>         , jitter_params=list(height=0, width=0)
>         , position="jitter"
>         )
> print(
>         ggplot() + layer2
>         + scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=0, labels="")
>         )
> #       But there is lots of jitter!
>
> #       Although the shortcut position_jitter() is documented, I have found no
> #       documentation for the full general syntax that uses layer() and position=jitter.
>
> What is going on? How do I make the jitter in one or both directions zero?

I'm not familiar with the syntax you are using (in particular, I don't
think "jitter_params" does anything).  One way to write it would be:

layer2<-layer(
         data=DAAT
         , mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
         , geom="point"
         , geom_params=list(shape=1)

         , position=position_jitter(width=0, height=0)
         )

I agree with you that qplot, whlle an easy-to-use interface to get
started, is somewhat confusing once you are doing more complicated
things.  I wouldn't use qplot in this case, but rather the full
ggplot() syntax to build up a layer manually.  If I were writing your
first example, I would probably do it something like this:

# "zero" column not necessary, just set aesthetic to 0 in the mapping!
DAAT <- data.frame( X=sort(exp(sample(rnorm(20), replace=T))))
# Use ggplot() call to set up data source and aesthetic mapping
ggplot(data=DAAT, mapping=aes(x=X, y=0)) +
# Create a point layer using geom_point, and set position to
position_jitter with desired parameters
geom_point(shape=I(1), position=position_jitter(width=0, height=9)) +
# Remove y-axis display by setting breaks=NA
scale_y_continuous(name="", breaks=NA)

Hope this is helpful!

Josh.

messages.subject: median_hilow with stat_summary seems broken
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A script I wrote a while ago seems to be broken under the versions of
packages I'm currently using. It seems to be an issue with the
median_hilow function that gets passed to stat_summary. I get the
following error:

Error: geom_crossbar requires the following missing aesthetics: ymax

And diving into things a bit I get:

> summary(mydata)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's
  0.000   5.000   8.000   9.508  12.000  80.000  12.000

> median_hilow(mydata, conf.int <http://conf.int>=.8)
  y y ymin
1 8 3   17

That seems weird. I would have expected that function to return values
of y, ymin, and ymax.

In debug:
debug: {
    try_require("Hmisc")
    result <- safe.call(fun, list(x = x, ...))
    rename(data.frame(t(result)), c(Median = "y", Mean = "y",
        Lower = "ymin", Upper = "ymax"))
}

> result
Median  Lower  Upper
     8      3     17

Ah, it appears as if it's pulling the version of rename() from plyr.
So, namespace issue maybe?

Versions:
R version 2.12.2 (2011-02-25)
x86_64-apple-darwin9.8.0
ggplot2   0.8.9
Hmisc     3.8-3
plyr        1.5.1
reshape

Any thoughts for fixes or workarounds? Upgrading to R 2.13.0 is not an
option...

 -Harlan

p <- arrangeGrob(qplot(1,1), textGrob("test"))

ggplot2:::.store$set(arrangeGrob(...))

should probably only return the last ggplot, nothing else. I'm happy

d1$col.factor<-NA

d1[d1$Value >= 0,]$col.factor<-"G"

ggplot(d1, aes(x=substr(Name,1,15), y=Value, fill = col.factor))+
geom_bar()+
theme_bw()+
opts(panel.border = theme_blank())+
scale_fill_manual(values=c("R"="red", "G"="green"))

B

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I'm not familiar with the ggpcp() function. I thus might have missed
more concise ways to do it. However, the following code seems to do
what you want.

require(ggplot2)

# create a new var with the car names
mtcars$car<-rownames(mtcars)

# melt the the data frame and rescale it
# this is identical to the transformations done by the ggpcp()
function
mmtcars <- melt(mtcars, measure = 2:6)
mmtcars <- ddply(mmtcars, 'variable', transform, value=
rescaler(value, type='range'))

# plot it
ggplot(aes(x= variable, y = value, col=mpg), data=mmtcars) +
	geom_point(size=I(5), alpha = I(0.3)) +
	geom_line(aes(group=car), alpha=I(0.5), data=subset(mmtcars, car %in%
c('Volvo 142E', 'Fiat X1-9')))

HTH

Matthieu

messages.subject: Re: facet_grid problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Endre,

This issue is you have chosen a function name as a variable name.
This can cause havoc in formulae.  For future reference, it is nice to
include a small example dataset.  This code demonstrates what I mean.
Notice that the variables "subset" and "altname" are the same
information, but different names.  Someone else may, but I do not
actually know a direct way around this short of renaming the variable.

Cheers,

Josh

set.seed(10)
dat <- data.frame(
  number = sample(1:100, 500, TRUE),
  promoter = factor(sample(1:3, 500, TRUE)),
  subset = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = 125)),
  altname = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = 125)))

require(ggplot2)

ggplot(dat, aes(number, fill=..count..)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_grid(promoter ~ subset)

ggplot(dat, aes(number, fill=..count..)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_grid(promoter ~ altname)

messages.subject: Re: quoted class in ddply, not in melt
messages.subject_clean: quoted class in ddply, not in melt
messages.body_plain:
Dear Hadley,

Thank you for your email on this subject.

As you develop and redesign the libraries, do you plan to document the "." function?

It seems that "." needs a help file that will plainly state *what it is intended for* and (on a more detail-oriented or nerdy plane) exactly what it does in terms of arguments and value returned. Like the traditional R help files.

By trial and error, I think I figured out that "." saves us from having to type quotation marks. But is that its point?

If I understand your post, you say that "." is also a way to rename the columns of a data frame.

If I want to rename the "pig" column to "pi", I do the following, which makes things explicit.

names(junk)[names(junk)=="pig"] <-"pi"

As an end-user, I am puzzled by why these operations (placing double quotes around strings and renaming columns of a dataframe) would be combined into a single function and why the function would be called dot (".") rather than an evocative mnemonic name.

One of my goals in writing R code is that I want to understand a year later what my code is supposed to do. I am scared to call a mysterious or obscure function because later on I might never figure out how my function works.

And a dot is very easy to miss if I'm reading through code. And one false keystroke would delete it.

But you must have something in mind with the "dot" function. It must be part of a more general plan for these libraries?  And you must have a darn good reason you call it dot?

Just my feedback

Jacob A. Wegelin
Assistant Professor
Department of Biostatistics
Virginia Commonwealth University
730 East Broad Street Room 3006
P. O. Box 980032
Richmond VA 23298-0032
U.S.A.
E-mail: jacobw...@fastmail.fm
URL: http://www.people.vcu.edu/~jwegelin

On Tue, 19 Apr 2011, Hadley Wickham wrote:

> On Mon, Apr 18, 2011 at 4:33 PM, Jacob Wegelin <jacobw...@fastmail.fm> wrote:
>>
>> ddply knows about the "quoted" class, which has the consequence (I think)
>> that one can use the following syntax to tell it which variables to use for
>> splitting:
>>
>> # Try printing
>> .( myonefactor, myotherfactor)
>>
>> # Turn this into something more familiar:
>> unlist(lapply(.( myonefactor, myotherfactor), paste))
>>
>> # Example of how this strange thing works:
>>
>> junk<-data.frame( pig=c("ee", "ee", "onk", "onk", "onk"), dog=c("uff",
>> "arg", "uff", "arg", "snarl"))
>> # junk<-rbind(junk, junk[2:4,])
>> junk$Y<-rnorm(nrow(junk))
>> require(ggplot2)
>> # An older way to think about it:
>> ddply(junk, c("pig", "dog"), function(STUFF) c(nrow=nrow(STUFF),
>> mean=mean(STUFF$Y)) )
>> # The "quoted class" way:
>> ddply(junk, .(pig, dog) , function(STUFF) c(nrow=nrow(STUFF),
>> mean=mean(STUFF$Y)) )
>
> But . does much more than that:
>
> f <- function(STUFF) c(nrow=nrow(STUFF), mean=mean(STUFF$Y))
>
> ddply(junk, .(dog = pig, pig = dog), f)
> ddply(junk, .(substr(pig, 1, 2)), f)
> ddply(junk, .(pi = substr(pig, 1, 2)), f)
>
>> # This seems to be related to the fact that the arguments of ddply (their
>> names) all start with a dot....?
>
> That's just a coincidence.
>
>> # This syntax does not work however in melt. The old way works:
>> melt(junk, id.vars=c("pig", "dog"))
>> # but the new way generates an error:
>> melt(junk, id.vars=.(pig, dog))
>>
>> # What's the thinking here?
>
> Basically, it makes sense to aggregate by computed values, but I don't
> think that it makes sense to melt by computed values.
>
> Hadley
>
> --
> Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
> Department of Statistics / Rice University
> http://had.co.nz/
>

messages.body_plain:
For the first 3 graphs you're dividing your dataset into different colors or different graphs by a factor that your example dataset does not have.

To do a 2D density plot you could do the following.

ggplot(x, aes(duration, pitch)) +
  stat_density2d(geom = "tile", aes(fill = ..density..), contour = F) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colour = c("darkblue", "lightblue", "green", "yellow", "orange", "red"), legend=F)

grid.arrange() from gridExtra should allow you to arrange all the plots in a stacked manner, you just need to build each one first and then put them together.
http://code.google.com/p/gridextra/

There have been posts here recently on aligning plots that should help you get things lined up well.

Brandon

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ista,

Thank you. That worked!

Group,

Unfortunately, having solved that issue, I've now run into a new one that escapes my intuition. Looking at the example below, it should be fairly clear what I'm trying to do. But two distinct problems get in my way:

1. How can I label a negative value in the appropriate position with its absolute value?
2. How can I apply a label format (e.g. comma) in conjunction with the absolute value function (i.e. geom_text(aes(label=comma(abs(x)))) doesn't seem to work)?

Below is where the solution stands now, with neither issue 1 or 2 solved:

 tst<-data.frame(age=rnorm(2000,50,30),gender=c(rep("f",1000),rep("m",1000)))

ggplot(data=subset(tst), aes(age)) +
geom_bar(data=subset(tst,gender=="f"),stat="bin",colour="pink",alpha=.3)+
geom_bar(data=subset(tst,gender=="m"),stat="bin",aes(y=-..count..),colour="blue",alpha=.3)+
coord_flip()+
theme_bw()+
geom_text(data=subset(tst,gender=="f"),stat="bin",aes(label=abs(..count..)),hjust=1)+
geom_text(data=subset(tst,gender=="m"),stat="bin",aes(label=abs(-..count..)),hjust=1)

Obviously, I'm in no way tied to using geom_bar - maybe geom_ribbon is the way to go here? But I think in any case, there is the requirement to label negative values with absolute values, positioned appropriately, as well as the need to apply a format (comma) function in addition to the abs function. And neither of these I've been able to figure out how to do.

Thanks for your help !

Adam Loveland

Tony Bigbee

now.

messages.subject: Re: Change colors in stat_binhex
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

How about something like this?

d <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price))

d + stat_binhex(aes(fill = cut(..count.., c(0, 50, 100, 500, 1000,
3000, 5000, 100000),
                                labels = c('0-50', '51-100',
'101-500', '501-1000',
                                           '1001-3000', '3001-5000',
'5000+')))) +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(fill = 'Count') +
    scale_fill_brewer(type = 'seq', pal = 'OrRd')

The idea is to use the cut() function on the counts to create a factor
variable with specified cut points and associated labels. I set seven
levels for the factor, so Brewer palette schemes are workable. You may
well prefer another color scheme, but this should show the basic idea.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: adjusting axis text position with facet_wrap
messages.subject_clean: adjusting axis text position with facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
Hi Denis,

The following represents my understanding, and could well be wrong.
I'm sure someone will quickly correct me if that is the case.

The basic misunderstanding here is that vjust and hjust are not
intended to (v)ertically ad(just) or (h)orizontially ad(just) the
text. They are designed to set the (v)ertical (just)ification and
(h)orizontal (just)ification. Basically, they are continuous analogs
of aligning text left, center, right, top, middle, bottom. If you read
the help file you will see that they should be set to values between 0
and 1. See ?theme_text for reference.

Now, in reality it seems you can use them to adjust the position, by
passing values smaller than 0 or larger than 1, but that doing so
results in weird things happening. I wouldn't get too hung up on that,
because it's simply not how they were designed to work. If anything,
theme_text could return an error if vjust or hjust were set outside
the [0,1] interval.

HTH,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: adjusting axis text position with facet_wrap
messages.subject_clean: adjusting axis text position with facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ista,

You may be right, but in this case the analogy with basic R's adj parameter would be lost because adj is intended to "justify" text, but by using values outside the 0-1 interval you can also move text.

This said, there are reasons to think we should be able to use values outside the 0-1 interval with predictable results. For instance, the value of 7 is used in Hadley's own example. Furthermore, if we could ONLY use values within 0 and 1 to have predictable results, then we'd need another parameter to be able to control how far the axis text is from the axis. Finally, in my tests, vjust had no effect at all unless I also used a non-zero value for angle.

My feeling is that hjust and vjust are supposed to do what I wanted, but something is wrong with the implementation right now. This would explain why the example from <https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Axis-Attributes> is not repeatable.

Cheers,

Denis

messages.subject: Re: adjusting axis text position with facet_wrap
messages.subject_clean: adjusting axis text position with facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
I still think setting values outside [0,1] usually makes no sense, and
only serves to complicate things -- and the function is not documented
to work that way (and I don't think Hadley is responsible for the wiki
examples). I played around with it a bit, and the behavior of the
hjust and vjust makes intuitive sense to me, even though I can't quite
articulate the rules exactly. If you use labels longer than one
character it helps to see when and how things are justified. Then,
systematically change things so you can isolate each effect:

dat <- data.frame(x=c("Long label for X value one", "Long label for X
value 2"), y=c(100000, 100001))
p1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point()
p1

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=.5),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=.5))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=1, hjust=.5),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=1, hjust=.5))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=1),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=1))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle = 45),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(angle = 45))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=.5, angle = 45),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=.5, angle = 45))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=1, hjust=.5, angle = 45),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=1, hjust=.5, angle = 45))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=1, angle = 45),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=1, angle = 45))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=.5, angle = 90),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=.5, angle = 90))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=1, hjust=.5, angle = 90),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=1, hjust=.5, angle = 90))

p1 + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=1, angle = 90),
          axis.text.y=theme_text(vjust=.5, hjust=1, angle = 90))

Wow, that was boring and lame. Sorry. Anyway, it makes sense to me.
Now what is is you want to do? What is the problem with the way the
theme_text settings work?

Best,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
Doing so would mean that gridExtra would replicate the code in ggsave
and last_plot with very minor changes, which is never good. I would
argue that a better solution would be to extract the part of ggsave
that isn't specific to ggplot2 and place it in a more generic package
that could be accessed by all grid-related packages. Not sure where
though, since R-base probably wouldn't want the burden, and ggplot2
would require it as a dependency.

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Ploting geom_line with missing values
messages.body_plain:
Remember: Please provide a reproducible example: http://gist.github.com/270442

# Some data that may look like yours:
ds <- data.frame(RTime = rep(letters[1:5], each = 5),
 Treatment = rep(paste("t", 1:5, sep = ""), 5), mean = rnorm(25))

# put in some missing means
ds[c(15, 10, 8, 1, 7, 11, 4, 5, 6, 13), "mean"] <- NA

# current plot
qplot(factor(RTime),mean,data=ds,color=Treatment)

# illustrates the problem?
qplot(factor(RTime),mean,data=ds,color=Treatment, geom = "line")

# you need to specify group since your x values are factors
qplot(factor(RTime),mean,data=ds,color=Treatment, geom = "line", group
 =  Treatment)
# but this doesn't solve the problem

# a missing point, NA, will break a line so,
# I think the easiest way is to get rid of the missing rows then plot:
ds.no.missing <- subset(ds, !is.na <http://is.na>(mean))
qplot(factor(RTime),mean,data=ds.no.missing,color=Treatment,na.rm=T,
geom = "line", group = Treatment) +
  geom_point()

Hope that helps,
Charlotte

messages.subject: Re: Change colors in stat_binhex
messages.body_plain:
To keep a continuous scale, another option is to grab the palette from
brewer and use scale_fill_gradientn:

library(RColorBrewer)

p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price)) + stat_binhex()
p + scale_fill_gradientn(colours = brewer.pal(9, "OrRd"))

# although with the diamonds data this is more revealing
p + scale_fill_gradientn(colours = brewer.pal(9, "OrRd"), trans = "log10")

Charlotte

messages.body_plain:
Dear Charlotte,

First thanks for Your time and suggestions.
Yes this indeed illustrates my problem, however skipping NAs is very wrong, because then You're not anymore comparing correct values for given x.  This plot will be misleading in any case of ordered measurement for which You have index on x axis.
For example You could draw a very wrong conclusion about significant difference at index-es which are really different, while thinking that they are the same.

What I would like to achieve is to connect two available points with a straight line (to observe pattern), with correct fixed x indexes on x-axis. This is re-occurring problem for me, which I haven't solved yet with ggplot2.

I would be very grateful if someone would knew how to make exactly such a plot.

Thanks
Mateusz

messages.subject: Can ggfluctuation automatic detect labels from table?
messages.subject_clean: Can ggfluctuation automatic detect labels from table?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

ggfluctuation label the axis as x and y. I could use xlab and ylab to
add the axis label manually according to the table dirnames. I think
that it may make more sense to label the axis according to the table's
dimnames. Could you let me know if ggfluctuation can figure out the
labels by itself?

###########

library(ggplot2)

m=3
n=5
adf=data.frame(
  Y1=sample(m,100,replace=T)
  , X1=sample(n,100,replace=T)
  )

tb=table(adf)

ggfluctuation(tb)
#ggfluctuation(tb)+xlab('X1')+ylab('Y1')

--
Regards,
Peng

label.cluster <- function(variable, value) {
    if (variable == 'platform') {
        levels(value)[which(levels(value) == 'emulab')] <- 'Emulab'
        levels(value)[which(levels(value) == 'g5k')] <- 'Grid 5000'
    }
    return(value)
}

    format(x/1000, big.mark=TRUE, scientific=FALSE, ...)
